01.note: King Yannai returned from conquering sixty cities in the desert and, in his joy, invited all the Sages to eat salty foods on tables of gold, in memory of their poor ancestors who ate such food while building the Temple. A scoffer, Elazar ben Po'ira, told him the Pharisees were secretly against him and urged him to make them stand before him while he wore the High Priest's frontplate. An elder, Yehuda ben Gedidya, then told Yannai to leave the priesthood to Aaron's descendants, since it was said his mother had been taken captive; the rumor was investigated and not confirmed, and the Sages were expelled in the king's rage. Elazar urged him to crush them, all the Sages were killed, and the world was desolate until Shimon ben Shatah restored the Torah.
01.why: Abaye holds that a single witness is believed about a wife's adultery and Rava disagrees. Abaye cites this account because the rumor about Yannai's mother was 'investigated and not found', which he reads as one witness believed unless two contradict him.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: A king who also serves as High Priest; he feasts with the Sages and then turns on them.

people.name: Elazar ben Po'ira
people.about: A scoffer, called evil-hearted and a scoundrel, who turns the king against the Sages.

people.name: Yehuda ben Gedidya
people.about: An elder who tells Yannai to give up the priesthood because of the rumor about his mother.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who comments that heresy entered Yannai at that moment.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: Restores the Torah after the Sages are killed.

terms.meaning: The gold plate engraved with God's name that the High Priest wore on his forehead.
Here, another name for the Sages.
The teachings handed down by the Sages alongside the written Bible. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak notes that, unlike a scroll in the corner, it cannot survive without them.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishnah, the core collection of Jewish law.

02.note: A man from Neharde'a, told at a butcher shop in Pumbedita to wait until Rav Yehuda's servant had been served, mocked Rav Yehuda with an insulting nickname. Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and, told that the man habitually called people slaves, proclaimed that he himself was a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court, and Rav Huna advised him to go out of respect for the Exilarch's house. At Rav Nahman's home Rav Yehuda corrected nearly everything his host said: his words for a fence, a bench, a citron and a cup, his offer to have his daughter Donag pour drinks, and his offer to send greetings to his wife Yalta. Yalta sent word to Rav Nahman to finish with him. How the case itself ended is not told here.
02.why: The Gemara has just quoted the teaching that whoever calls others flawed in lineage is himself flawed, with Shmuel's comment; this man, who called people slaves, is the case where Rav Yehuda acted on it.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Yehezkel
people.about: A Sage in Pumbedita whose servant is served first; he excommunicates the man and declares him a slave.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a before whom the man summons Rav Yehuda.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Advises Rav Yehuda to answer the summons.

people.name: Donag
people.about: Rav Nahman's daughter, a minor.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Nahman's wife, who tells him to end the exchange.

terms.meaning: To put a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia. Rav Nahman was linked to his household, so ignoring Rav Nahman's summons would slight it.
Saying a man descends from non-Jewish slaves, which meant he could not marry a Jew of unflawed lineage.

02.flag: The story stops before the hearing: Rav Nahman's questioning and its outcome begin in the following segments, which appear as a separate story (0D736B).

03.note: Rav Yehuda has come to Rav Nahman's court in Neharde'a, summoned by a man he excommunicated and declared a slave. He explained that the man had insulted a Sage's agent and habitually called people slaves. The man arrived, protesting that he came from the Hasmonean kings; Rav Yehuda quoted Shmuel that anyone who says so is a slave. When Rav Nahman objected to a ruling quoted after the fact, Rav Mattana, arriving that day after thirteen years away, confirmed it: the last Hasmonean girl had cried this from a roof, then fell and died. The man was proclaimed a slave and several marriage contracts were torn up. Townspeople chased Rav Yehuda to stone him; he threatened to reveal Shmuel's list of flawed families, and they threw down the stones, which dammed the Malka River.
03.why: The Gemara is listing families of flawed lineage; in this hearing Rav Nahman presses whether Shmuel's teaching lets one only suspect a man who calls others slaves, or also proclaim him one.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage from Pumbedita, summoned to court for declaring a man a slave.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge in Neharde'a who hears the case.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage, back in Neharde'a after thirteen years, who confirms what Shmuel said.

terms.meaning: A royal family of priests. In Shmuel's teaching, none of them survived except slaves and one girl, so a claim to descend from them marks a man as a slave.
The document a husband gives his wife at marriage (ketubah). Tearing them up meant those marriages were treated as invalid.
To put a person under a formal ban that cuts him off from the community.

03.flag: The story begins mid-scene: the insult, the summons and the dinner exchange that lead into it are in the preceding segments (story 4AB242).

04.note: In Rabbi Pinehas's day, people wanted to declare the lineage of Babylonian families doubtful compared to the Land of Israel's. Rabbi Pinehas told his servants that once he had made two statements in the house of study, they should pick him up on a stretcher and run. He first announced that slaughtering a bird is not required by Torah law, and while the scholars were absorbed in that, he declared that the Land of Israel's lineage is muddled compared to Babylonia's. His servants carried him off, and his pursuers could not catch him. The scholars then examined families' lineage until they reached ones too dangerous to accuse, and stopped.
04.why: The Gemara has just quoted the teaching that Babylonian lineage is purer than the Land of Israel's, and told how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi resisted the opposite claim; this is a second attempt at that claim, met the same way.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas
people.about: A Sage who declares the Land of Israel's lineage muddled compared to Babylonia's, then has himself carried away.

terms.meaning: Family descent. A flaw in it, such as descent from a forbidden union, could bar a person from marrying into other families.
Mixed with families of doubtful descent, so that marrying into them would require checking first.
The hall where the Sages and their students met to learn and debate.

05.note: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian Sage, kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan of the Land of Israel, who kept asking him to marry his daughter. One day on the road, Ze'eiri lifted Rabbi Yohanan onto his shoulders and carried him across a large puddle. Rabbi Yohanan said: our Torah is fit in your eyes, but our daughters are not? He argued that if Ze'eiri feared the flawed families who had come up from Babylonia, some must have stayed behind in Babylonia too. The Gemara comments that Rabbi Yohanan had missed Rabbi Elazar's teaching that Ezra left Babylonia only after making it pure like fine flour. Ze'eiri's reply is not given.
05.why: The Gemara has just said that anyone who speaks like a Babylonian may marry without having his lineage checked, since Babylonian families are presumed unflawed; here a Babylonian Sage holds back from marrying into a family of the Land of Israel.

people.name: Ze'eiri
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who avoids marrying Rabbi Yohanan's daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who keeps offering his daughter to Ze'eiri.

terms.meaning: A passage of the Mishnah, the core early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses.
A mishna lists ten classes of Jews by descent who came up from Babylonia with Ezra, from priests and Levites down to those of flawed lineage.

06.note: Ulla visited Rav Yehuda in Pumbedita and saw that his son, Rav Yitzhak, was grown but unmarried. Asked why, Rav Yehuda said he did not know where he could find a wife for him. Ulla answered that none of them could be sure of their own descent: they might come from the women ravished in Zion, or from the people the prophet Amos describes lying on ivory beds, whom Rabbi Abbahu explains as men who swapped wives. When Rav Yehuda asked what to do, Ulla told him to go by silence, as the people of the Land of Israel do: when two people quarrel, the one who falls silent first is of finer lineage.
06.why: The Gemara is discussing how to know which families have unflawed lineage; Ulla's advice gives a practical test, which Rav then applies to Babylonia in the lines that follow.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A visitor to Pumbedita who questions Rav Yehuda and advises him.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Ulla's host, who fears he cannot find a wife of sure lineage for his son.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak
people.about: Rav Yehuda's son, grown and still unmarried.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose reading of the verse in Amos Rabbi Abbahu ridicules.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage who offers a harsher reading of the verse in Amos.

terms.meaning: The Babylonian Sages' name for the Land of Israel.
Family descent. A flaw in it, such as descent from adultery, could bar a person from marrying into other families.

07.note: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd pelted him with their etrogim. Rava said no one should teach such a thing where converts are common. Rava himself then taught there that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he later taught them that a convert may marry a mamzeret, they told him he had spoiled his first teaching. Rava answered that he had done them good: a convert may marry from either group, as he wishes.
07.why: The Gemara has just cited support for Rav's view that priests' daughters may marry men barred from the priesthood, after debating whether converts may marry a mamzeret; Rava's two teachings state both rulings, which the Gemara then adopts as law.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who criticizes Rabbi Zeira and then teaches both rulings himself.

terms.meaning: A person born outside the Jewish people who has joined it.
A woman born of a forbidden union such as adultery or incest. She may not marry most Jews.
Citrons, the fruit held during the festival of Sukkot; the crowd evidently had them in hand.

08.note: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host, the son of a convert, quarreled with Rav Beivai over which of them would hold an official post in the city. They came before Rav Yosef, who cited the verse about appointing a king 'from among your brothers' to rule that every appointment must go to someone from among the Jewish people. Rav Adda bar Ahava asked whether that applies even when the mother was born Jewish; Rav Yosef said such a man counts as 'from among your brothers'. So Rav Beivai, a great scholar, would oversee the city's religious matters and the host its other affairs. Abaye remarked that whoever hosts a scholar should host one like Rav Adda bar Ahava, who knows how to argue in his favor.
08.why: The mishna says anyone whose ancestors held public posts may marry into the priesthood without checking, and the Gemara asks whether people of flawed lineage are ever appointed; this case shows who may hold a post.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Ahava
people.about: A Sage whose question wins his host the appointment.

people.name: Rav Beivai
people.about: A great scholar who competes with the host for the post.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who decides between them.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who draws the moral about hosting scholars.

terms.meaning: A person born outside the Jewish people who has joined it. Here the host's father was a convert and his mother was born Jewish.

09.note: A woman came to Jerusalem carrying a child on her shoulders, and she raised him. He later had intercourse with her, and they were brought to court and stoned. The report, passed down in bar Kappara's name, stresses that it was not certain he was her son; he had clung to her, and that was enough.
09.why: Rabbi Yohanan holds that a court may flog, stone or burn on the basis of presumed status alone, without witnesses to the family tie; this incident is cited as a death sentence resting on such a presumption.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: The Sage in whose name the incident is reported.

terms.meaning: What everyone takes to be true from how people live, here that a boy who clung to a woman was her son.
Stoning was one of the death penalties a Jewish court could impose, here for intercourse between mother and son.

10.note: Captive women who had been brought to Neharde'a were lodged in the upper room of Rav Amram the Pious, and the ladder was taken away. When one of them passed the opening, it was as though a light shone through it. Rav Amram seized a ladder that ten men could not lift and began to climb. Halfway up he braced himself and cried out: Fire in the house of Amram! The Sages came and said he had shamed them; he answered that it was better to be shamed in this world than in the World-to-Come. He made his evil inclination leave him, and it came out like a pillar of fire. He told it: you are fire and I am flesh, and still I am stronger than you.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing how to keep men and women from being alone together, with Abaye and Rava setting up barriers and Avin warning that festivals are the dangerous time; this story shows even a pious Sage nearly overcome.

people.name: Rav Amram the Pious
people.about: The Sage who hosts the captive women and overcomes his desire halfway up the ladder.

terms.meaning: Jewish women taken prisoner and then freed, usually by being ransomed.
The urge to do wrong, pictured here as a force that can be made to leave a person.
The life after this one, where people are judged for how they lived.

11.note: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far side of a river. There was no ferry, so he took hold of a rope bridge and started across. Halfway over, it left him and said that if heaven were not proclaiming 'Be careful with Rabbi Meir and his Torah', it would have made his blood worth two ma'a.
11.why: The Gemara is discussing the pull of temptation between men and women; after Rav Amram's struggle it tells of Sages who scoffed at sinners and were shown how close they came to falling.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who mocked sinners until he was tempted himself.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Appears to Rabbi Meir as a woman across the river.

terms.meaning: A small coin. Blood worth two ma'a means a life made worthless.
Here the same as the evil inclination, the tempter who lures a person to sin; the story uses both names.

12.note: Rabbi Akiva also used to mock sinners. One day Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree. He took hold of the tree and began to climb. Halfway up, it left him and said that if heaven were not proclaiming 'Be careful with Rabbi Akiva and his Torah', it would have made his blood worth two ma'a.
12.why: This is the second of a run of stories, after Rabbi Meir's, about Sages who scoffed at sinners and were shown how close they came to falling, in a discussion of the pull of temptation between men and women.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who mocked sinners until he was tempted himself.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Appears to Rabbi Akiva as a woman at the top of a palm tree.

terms.meaning: A small coin. Blood worth two ma'a means a life made worthless.
Here the same as the evil inclination, the tempter who lures a person to sin; the story uses both names.

13.note: The Sage Peleimu used to say every day: An arrow in Satan's eye. On the eve of Yom Kippur, Satan came to his door as a poor man. Peleimu gave him bread, then at his complaints brought him inside and seated him at the table, where he sat covered in boils and pus, behaving repulsively. Given a cup, he spat phlegm into it; when they scolded him, he collapsed and seemed to die, and people cried: Peleimu killed a man! Peleimu fled and hid in the bathroom. Satan followed and fell before him, and seeing him suffer, revealed himself. Asked what he should say instead, Peleimu was told: May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.
13.why: This follows the accounts of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva, who mocked sinners and were tested; here a Sage who taunts Satan daily is taught to ask God to rebuke him instead.

people.name: Peleimu
people.about: A Sage who taunted Satan every day.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Comes to Peleimu disguised as a poor man and torments him.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, a fast day; the day before it is marked by a festive meal.
A name for God.

14.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi prayed every time he fell on his face in prayer: May the Merciful One save us from the evil inclination. His wife heard and wondered why, since he had kept away from her for years. One day, while he studied in his garden, she adorned herself and walked back and forth past him, saying she was Haruta, returning from her day. He propositioned her; she asked for a pomegranate from the top of a tree, he brought it, and they had intercourse. At home, his wife was lighting the oven and he climbed in and sat inside it. When she said it had been her, he ignored her until she gave him signs. He said: I, in any case, intended to sin. All his days he fasted, until he died by that death.
14.why: Right after this, the Gemara shows from verses that one who meant to sin needs atonement even if no sin took place; Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi's lifelong fasting puts that idea into a life.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi
people.about: A Sage who prays to be saved from temptation and falls for his own disguised wife.

people.name: Haruta
people.about: The name his wife gives while disguised; the translation explains it as a prostitute's name.

terms.meaning: A posture of private prayer, bowing low with the face covered.
The urge to do wrong, especially sexual temptation in this story.

15.note: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and placed his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he did not think she might already be betrothed. Rav Aha replied that if so, Rav Hisda had broken Rav's rule against betrothing a daughter while she is a minor, before she can say whom she wants. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha was breaking Shmuel's rule that one may not make use of a woman. Rav Aha answered that he followed another saying of Shmuel: everything is permitted when done for the sake of Heaven.
15.why: The Gemara is discussing how close a man may be to young relatives, and Rav Hisda has just ruled that a father may not sleep near a daughter once she is ashamed before him; this story shows where affection toward a granddaughter stands.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Abba
people.about: Rav Hisda's father-in-law, who holds his granddaughter on his lap.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The son-in-law he is visiting, who questions him.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, after which a woman is legally bound to her husband. A father could betroth his daughter while she was still a minor.
Being served or attended by a woman, which Shmuel forbade as too intimate.
Done with pure intentions, here out of family affection with no hint of desire.

16.note: Bar Haddaya was to deliver a bill of divorce from one country to another and asked Rabbi Ahai, who was in charge of bills of divorce, how to proceed. Rabbi Ahai told him he had to stand over every single letter as it was written. Bar Haddaya then asked Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, who told him he did not need to. The answer goes on: if he chose to be strict anyway, he would be casting doubt on the bills of divorce delivered before.
16.why: The Gemara has been discussing the agent's declaration that a bill of divorce was written and signed in his presence; this case asks how closely he must actually watch the writing to make it.

people.name: Bar Haddaya
people.about: An agent about to deliver a bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai
people.about: The Sage in charge of bills of divorce, who demands strict supervision.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: One of two Sages who tell Bar Haddaya he need not watch every letter.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: One of two Sages who tell Bar Haddaya he need not watch every letter.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.

17.note: Rabba bar bar Hana brought a bill of divorce, half of which had been written in his presence and half not. He asked Rabbi Elazar, who told him that if the scribe wrote even one line of it for the woman's sake in his presence, nothing more was needed. Rav Ashi said that even hearing the sound of the quill and the parchment is enough.
17.why: This continues the question of how much of the writing an agent must witness to declare that a bill of divorce was written in his presence; the teaching cited next is brought as support for Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: An agent who saw only half of a bill of divorce being written.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: The Sage who tells him one line written in his presence is enough.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who says even hearing the writing is enough.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
A bill of divorce must be written specifically for this woman, not prepared as a blank form.

18.note: Rav Hanin reports that Rav Kahana brought a bill of divorce, either from Sura to Neharde'a or the other way round; Rav Hanin did not know which. Rav Kahana asked Rav whether he had to declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence. Rav told him he did not have to.
18.why: The Gemara has been asking how far a bill of divorce must travel before the agent has to make this declaration; in the lines that follow, Rav's answer goes on to say that making it anyway protects the divorce if the husband contests it.

people.name: Rav Hanin
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: An agent bringing a bill of divorce.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage Rav Kahana asks.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
Two Jewish towns in Babylonia.

18.flag: The story stops mid-sentence: Rav's answer continues in the next segment ('but if you do, you provide benefit').

19.note: A man brought a bill of divorce before Rabbi Yishmael and asked whether he had to declare that it was written and signed in his presence. Rabbi Yishmael asked where he was from, and on hearing 'the village of Sisai', told him to make the declaration, so that he would not need witnesses. After the man left, Rabbi Elai objected that Sisai lies within the Land of Israel, closer to Tzippori than Akko is, so the declaration was not needed. Rabbi Yishmael told him: Be silent, my son, be silent; since the matter went out as permitted, it went out.
19.why: The Gemara has just explained that an agent who makes the declaration even when not required means the husband's later challenge is ignored; this incident is cited as the source.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage who tells the man to make the declaration.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: A Sage who questions why the declaration was needed.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. When one is delivered from abroad, the agent who brings it must declare: It was written in my presence and signed in my presence.
A city at the edge of the Land of Israel; Rabbi Meir rules it counts as the Land of Israel for bills of divorce.
A city in the heart of the Land of Israel.

20.note: Rabbi Evyatar met Elijah the prophet and asked him what God was doing. Elijah said God was studying the story of the concubine in Gibeah, saying: Evyatar My son says this, and Yonatan My son says that. Rabbi Evyatar protested: God forbid, is there uncertainty before Heaven? Elijah answered that both are the words of the living God: the husband found a fly and did not take offense, then found a hair and did.
20.why: Rabbi Evyatar's standing as a Sage has just been questioned, and Abaye defends him by saying God agreed with his reading; this meeting with Elijah is the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Evyatar
people.about: A Sage who asks Elijah what God is doing.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who reports what God is studying.

people.name: God
people.about: Described as studying the passage and quoting both Sages.

people.name: Yonatan
people.about: The Sage whose opposing reading God also quotes.

terms.meaning: The story in Judges 19 of a woman who left her husband, which led to a terrible war; the Sages disputed what had angered him.

terms.term: these and those are the words of the living God
terms.meaning: Both opinions are true; here, both incidents happened.
